Re-ran the component spec fresh (10/10 pass) and the full consumer-app suite (149 files / 984 tests, all green). Nothing in this area has changed since 2026-07-29.
- [x] Subscription refund — same, specifically for the "any usage ledger CONSUME entry, even if later restored" permanent-ineligibility rule already implemented. **Backend logic confirmed correct and already properly unit-tested; found and fixed a real bug in the customer-facing UI — e2e-bug.187 below.** Unlike bookings/packages, `ServiceSubscriptionsService.cancelSubscription` (`service-subscriptions.service.ts:128`) already returns an explicit `'ineligible'` status (not just `undefined`) — confirmed via source and the existing `isRefundEligible reflects usage even after a later restore` unit test, which mocks the ledger count directly to prove the rule holds regardless of any later restore (the count query filters `action: CONSUME` only, so a subsequent `RESTORE` row never reduces it — a permanent flag by design). The AI-assistant `cancel_my_subscription` intent (`ai-self-service-booking.logic.ts:749`) already branches correctly on all 4 outcomes including a clear, specific ineligible message ("...it isn't eligible for a refund"). **e2e-bug.187**: the actual consumer-app UI component (`ConsumerSubscriptionsSection.tsx`), which is the one real customers use (not the AI intent), had the exact same silent-swallow bug as e2e-bug.185/186 — `handleCancel()` only checked `if (result.refundStatus === 'refunded')`, so `'ineligible'` and `'failed'` were both silently dropped: a customer whose membership had genuinely been used (and was correctly *not* refunded) saw no explanation at all, identical to a customer whose refund had failed outright. Fixed by capturing the full result and branching on `'refunded'` / `'failed'` / `'ineligible'`, adding two new copy keys (`subscriptionsCancelRefundFailed`, `subscriptionsCancelIneligible`, all 3 locales) since no existing string covered these cases. Verified with 4 new unit tests (`ConsumerSubscriptionsSection.spec.tsx`): refunded, failed, ineligible, and no-notice-when-absent, all passing; `tsc --noEmit` clean; full suite 148 files / 970 tests green; confirmed live that the account page still renders with no console errors after the change.

  **Found and left undecided/not fixed — a second, more structural gap in the same component**: the Cancel button's own visibility check, `isUnused = sub.status === 'active' && sub.appointmentsRemaining === included`, is a *balance*-based heuristic, not the ledger-based one the backend actually uses. If a customer consumes one visit (a real `CONSUME` row) and that credit is later restored (e.g. the booking that consumed it gets cancelled, via `restoreCreditForBooking`), `appointmentsRemaining` returns to `included` and the Cancel button reappears — even though the backend will still correctly return `'ineligible'` on an actual cancel attempt (the CONSUME row never goes away). So a customer in this specific state sees a normal, unqualified "Cancel subscription" button, clicks it expecting a refund (nothing in the UI hints otherwise beforehand), and only learns it's ineligible *after* confirming the irreversible cancellation — the e2e-bug.187 fix at least ensures they're told why at that point, but the button itself oversells eligibility going in. Not fixed here: correcting it properly means threading a real eligibility signal (e.g. `isRefundEligible`) through `listCustomerSubscriptions`'s response into `PublicCustomerSubscription`, which is a backend API change, not a UI display fix — a larger, differently-scoped effort than this pass's bar for fixing narrow, contained bugs. Flagged for a future pass.
- [x] Gift-card refund/cancel-request — this one goes through a request/approval flow (`submitPublicGiftCardCancelRequest`) rather than an instant refund; confirm the pending-request state displays correctly and doesn't imply the refund already happened. **Checklist's own premise doesn't match the actual implementation — there is no manual approval step at all, and the UI is already correctly built. No bug found.** Read `GiftCardOrderService.submitCancelRequest` (`gift-card-order.service.ts:127`) in full: it creates a `GiftCardChangeRequest` row with `status: 'pending'`, but then — synchronously, in the same call, before ever responding — deactivates the card, calls `refundService.refundPurchase(...)` (Stripe refund attempt), and immediately flips the request row to `status: 'completed'` with a `resolvedAt` timestamp. Grepped the entire backend for a dashboard/staff-facing approve/reject endpoint for these requests — none exists. So despite the entity's naming (`GiftCardChangeRequest`, `status: 'pending' → 'completed'`, `customerNotes`) evoking a real human-review workflow, this is actually a fully automatic, instant cancel-and-refund — the "request" is really just an audit-trail record of an already-resolved action, confirmed by the existing unit test asserting `result.request.status` is `'completed'` (not `'pending'`) by the time `submitCancelRequest` returns. Consequence for the checklist's actual concern: there is no window in which the customer could see "pending" while a refund had secretly already happened, because the two are never out of sync — the request is only ever "pending" for the sub-millisecond it exists inside the transaction, and by the time any response reaches the customer it's already resolved to a definitive outcome. Confirmed the consumer-app UI (`ConsumerGiftCardsOrdersSection.tsx`) already handles this correctly (unlike the three sibling components that needed e2e-bug.185/186/187): `cancelOrder()` captures the real `refundStatus` and branches cleanly into `'refunded'`/`'already_refunded'` → green success copy ("Order cancelled and refunded."), `'failed'` → red failure copy ("Cancelled, but refund could not be processed."), else → a generic submitted-copy fallback — no silent swallowing anywhere. `getCustomerOrder`'s `changeRequest` field only surfaces requests in `OPEN_REQUEST_STATUSES` (i.e. still-pending ones), so a normal, successfully-resolved cancel never shows a stray "Request status: pending" line alongside its own success/failure message. **One narrow, hard-to-trigger gap noted, not fixed**: `submitCancelRequest` has no try/catch around the deactivate-card/refund/mark-completed sequence, so a genuine mid-transaction infrastructure failure (e.g. a DB write error between creating the pending row and completing it) would leave a request permanently stuck at `'pending'` — visible forever as "Request status: pending" with the Cancel button hidden (since `!order.changeRequest && policy.canCancel` gates it) and no retry path or guidance shown. This requires an actual database/infra fault mid-request to trigger, not a reachable user flow, so it wasn't live-reproduced or fixed — same bar applied to the double-cancel gap noted two items above.

#### Activation (first-time-user) payment-method defaulting

- [x] `resolveActivationPaymentMethod` — confirm the first-ever booking for a brand-new customer (or a deferred deep-link resume) defaults the payment method differently than a returning customer's booking, per the `n99-3.3` activation logic; identify exactly what that difference is (defaults to cash to reduce friction? defaults to online to capture payment info early? needs reading the rest of this function to know which). **Confirmed live: defaults to cash, specifically to reduce first-booking friction — but only under one of two A/B-tested variants, not unconditionally.** Read `activation-payment.util.ts` in full: `resolveActivationPaymentMethod` forces `paymentMethod = 'cash'` whenever `isActivationPath && cashAvailable`, **unless** `paymentTiming === 'online_first'`, in which case it leaves `currentMethod` untouched. `paymentTiming` (`'pay_at_venue_default' | 'online_first'`) turns out to be a stable, per-device 50/50 A/B experiment (`activation-path-ab.util.ts`'s `assignActivationPathVariants`, hashed from an anonymous device id, persisted in `localStorage`, overridable by a business-promoted winner via `activationPathAb` config) — not a business setting or a fixed default. So the actual behavior being tested is: does defaulting first-time bookers to "pay at the venue" (skip asking for card details entirely on their very first booking) improve activation/conversion, versus leaving payment method at whatever the checkout would otherwise default to? Confirmed live end-to-end: seeded `localStorage`'s `consumer_activation_path_variants` with `paymentTiming: 'pay_at_venue_default'`, cleared `consumer_completed_booking_count`, temporarily enabled `settings.publicBooking.acceptCashPayments` on the test business, and loaded a `prepaymentMode: 'none'` service's book page — the CTA read **"Confirm — pay at visit"** (`resolveCheckoutAmountLabel`'s `pay_at_visit` branch, which requires `paymentMethod === 'cash' && isActivationPath`), confirming the auto-cash-default fired on this fresh device. Also found and closed a real test-coverage gap while reading the function: the existing fixture file (`activation-payment.fixtures.ts`) had zero scenarios exercising the `paymentTiming: 'online_first'` branch at all — added 3 new cases (`activation-pay-at-venue-variant-defaults-cash`, `activation-online-first-variant-keeps-online`, `activation-online-first-variant-does-not-force-online`) proving the `online_first` variant is a no-op pass-through (doesn't force online either — it just disables the cash-forcing override, leaving whatever method was already selected). All pass; `tsc --noEmit` clean.

  **Bug found and fixed in passing (unrelated to activation logic, hit while setting up this test)**: my first attempt to toggle `acceptCashPayments` via `UPDATE businesses SET settings = jsonb_set(settings, '{acceptCashPayments}', 'true')` silently had no effect on the API response — traced to `resolvePublicPaymentSettings` (`customer-self-service.util.ts:77`) actually reading the flag from the **nested** `settings.publicBooking.acceptCashPayments`, not a top-level key. Not a genuine app bug (just my own wrong raw-SQL path this session), but confirms this nesting is easy to get wrong when touching business settings directly via SQL rather than through the dashboard UI — worth remembering for future direct-DB test setup in this business's `settings` jsonb column.
- [x] Confirm this activation-specific behavior doesn't leak into a customer's 2nd+ booking (i.e., `completedBookingCount` is read correctly and the special-casing genuinely turns off afterward). **Confirmed live, using the same test business/service/localStorage setup as the item above.** `completedBookingCount` (`store-review-prompt.util.ts`) is a purely device-local `localStorage` counter — not an account/backend-level count — incremented once via `incrementCompletedBookingCount()` immediately after any booking (single/multi/package/subscription) successfully confirms, inside `BookPage.tsx`'s shared success handler. This means "activation" really means "first successful booking *on this device*," not "first booking on this account" — a genuinely new customer who switches devices mid-relationship, or clears site data, would trigger the activation UX again; a returning customer on a shared/reused browser profile would not see it at all on an otherwise-first booking. This is a deliberate, reasonable proxy for the actual intent (nothing else is available client-side without an extra account-level API round-trip) and not treated as a bug. With the counter freshly cleared (simulating a real first-time device), the book page correctly showed "Confirm — pay at visit" (activation path, forced cash). Set `consumer_completed_booking_count` to `'1'` (simulating this exact device having completed one prior booking) and reloaded the identical service's book page: the CTA correctly reverted to plain **"Confirm booking"** — no forced cash, matching a normal returning-customer flow — confirming `isActivationBookingPath`'s `completedBookingCount === 0` check is read correctly and the special-casing genuinely, verifiably turns off after the first booking. (The one legitimate, intentional exception is `isDeferredResume`, which stays true regardless of `completedBookingCount` — already covered by the existing `deferred-resume` fixture scenario, correctly treating a resumed deep-link as activation-equivalent even for a technically-returning customer, which matches the intent described in the `n99-3.3` requirement itself.) No bug found.

#### Currency

- [x] Business currency vs. any display-currency conversion — confirm amounts shown at every step (quote, checkout, confirmation, account history) agree with each other and with what Stripe actually charges, for this business's configured currency (USD) and ideally a second business with a different currency if one exists in the seed data. **No actual currency conversion exists anywhere in the app — confirmed via full source read — and no second-currency business exists in this seed data. Amount agreement across the funnel is already independently proven by this session's own real Stripe transactions. One display completeness gap noted, not fixed.**

  **No second-currency business exists in the seed data.** Checked all 5 businesses (`GevGas operations`, 2× `QA Test Clinic`, `Pollin Clinic`, `QA Test Tours`) both via raw DB inspection and by calling each one's live public profile endpoint — every single one resolves to `currency: "USD"`. Traced why: none has ever set `settings.currency` (or the legacy `settings.defaultCurrency`, or `settings.locale.currency`) — `getBusinessDefaultCurrency` (`business-currency.util.ts:75`) falls through all three lookups and lands on its final hardcoded `return 'USD'`. Also confirmed every `services.currency` and `gift_cards.currency` row in the entire database is `USD` — zero entity-vs-business currency mismatches exist anywhere in this dataset today, so there's no live "disagreement" scenario to reproduce without first fabricating one.

  **There is no display-currency *conversion* to test — only currency-code *selection*.** Read `business-currency.ts` (consumer-app) and `business-currency.util.ts` (backend) in full: `resolveDisplayCurrency`/`resolvePriceCurrency` only ever pick *which* ISO code to label a number with (an entity's own currency if it's a recognized supported code, else falling back to the business's resolved currency) — there is no exchange-rate math anywhere, client or server. Every amount shown at every step is the same raw number, just formatted through `Intl.NumberFormat` with the resolved currency code (`formatConsumerPrice`/`formatPublicMoney` on the consumer-app side, `formatBusinessMoney` for dashboard KPIs). Grepped every consumer-app page/component for a hardcoded `'$'`/`"$"` literal that could bypass this and desync from a business's actual currency — none found; the one place a literal `$` was visually observed earlier this session (the loyalty-balance line, "$490.25 available") turned out to be `formatPublicMoney(amount, currency, tenantCurrency)`-formatted, not hardcoded, confirmed by reading `ConsumerCheckoutDiscounts.tsx`.

  **Funnel agreement is already independently proven, real-money-verified, from this session's own prior live Stripe tests** (not re-run here to avoid pointless repetition): the $40.00 "QA Concurrency Test" booking's quote (`amountDue: 40`), the Stripe Checkout session creation response (`amount: 40, currency: "USD"`), Stripe's own hosted page ($40.00), the actual captured `PaymentIntent` (`amount: 4000, amount_received: 4000` — cents, correctly ×100 from the $40.00 shown), and the subsequent refund (`re_...: amount: 4000`) all agree to the cent, confirmed by querying Stripe's API directly rather than trusting our own app's response. No disagreement found anywhere in this chain across the many real transactions run this session.

  **Stripe's own hosted Checkout page shows a second currency (AMD) — this is Stripe's feature, not ours, and doesn't affect what's actually charged.** Already observed and documented earlier this session: Stripe's Checkout page offers a "Choose a currency" toggle (e.g. "AMD 15,255.42 / $40.00") based on the customer's browser locale — purely a customer-facing display convenience on Stripe's own page. The actual `PaymentIntent`/charge is always created and captured in the business's configured currency (USD) regardless of which toggle the customer views; confirmed via the exact `amount`/`currency` fields on every real charge and refund pulled from Stripe's API this session. Worth stating explicitly since it could easily be mistaken for the app itself doing currency conversion — it isn't.

  **One completeness gap found, not fixed — "account history" shows no amount at all for plain bookings.** `ConsumerBookingActions.tsx` (the per-booking row component rendered in "My Bookings") never imports or calls any money-formatting utility and displays no price/amount for a booking, past or upcoming — confirmed via source (no `formatPublicMoney`/`formatConsumerPrice` import) and live (the account page's "My appointments" list shows only service name, provider, date, and status for every booking, never a price). This differs from gift cards' order-history section and the subscriptions section, both of which do show balance/amount. Since nothing is displayed, there's no numeric *disagreement* possible here — but it does mean a customer reviewing past bookings in-app has no way to confirm how much they paid for a specific visit without checking their card/bank statement or contacting the business. Flagged as a UI completeness observation for a possible future polish pass, not fixed here — out of scope for a currency-*agreement* correctness check.

### e2e-test-plan.consumer-app-payment-cases — All payment test cases, including AI-assistant-driven payment

Combines and extends the two prior deep-dives (`e2e-test-plan.consumer-app-online-payment` and `e2e-test-plan.consumer-app-ai-assistant`) at the user's request to cover "all payment cases including payment with AI assistant." Grounded in reading `backend/src/modules/ai/ai-payments.util.ts`/`ai-payments.logic.ts`/`ai-cash-payment-checkout.util.ts` and `consumer-app/src/lib/public-assistant-checkout.util.ts`/`consumer-gift-card-assistant-prefill.util.ts`.

**Blocking dependency, restated and sharpened:** the backend defines **18 distinct customer-facing payment intents** (`CUSTOMER_PAYMENTS_INTENTS` in `ai-payments.util.ts:116-134`) — every one of them routes through the same `/public/:slug/assistant` endpoint that **e2e-bug.1** crashes on the first hit. This bug is more consequential than previously scoped: it doesn't just block "chat with the assistant," it blocks an entire parallel payment-intent surface (quote-by-conversation, pay-by-conversation, receipt lookup by conversation) that has nothing to do with the regular checkout-page flows already covered.

**Execution note:** for the online-payment-specific cases (Stripe checkout, prepayment modes), use `pollin-clinic-3b7fb9d8` per the prior session's finding (real Stripe Connect account, all-`full`-prepayment services, gift cards enabled). For the pure conversational/classifier cases (does the assistant recognize the right intent for a given prompt), the original test business works fine once e2e-bug.1 is fixed, since those don't need real payment infrastructure — just a `sessionId`/quote to talk about.

#### The 18 customer payment intents — one section per intent

- [x] **`check_providers_for_service`** — "who's available for a haircut" — read-only, not really payment but gates entry into a paid booking; confirm it correctly surfaces prepayment-required info per provider/service if relevant. **Confirmed via full source read: it surfaces zero pricing/prepayment info, anywhere — not partially, not per-provider, not even in the structured `details` payload.** Read `handleCheckProvidersForServiceLogic` (`ai-payments.logic.ts:953`) and `buildCheckProvidersSummary` (`ai-provider-availability.util.ts:30`) in full: the response is built purely from `{ name, role, earliestDateKey, earliestStartTime, previewTimes }` per provider — no `price`, `prepaymentMode`, or `depositAmount` field is read from the resolved `service` object or threaded into either the human-readable summary text or the structured `details`/`availability` array returned to the client. This isn't a partial gap — it's a complete absence by design: prepayment mode is a service-level (not provider-level) property, and since this intent already requires a single resolved service to run at all, repeating "this service requires prepayment" on every availability check would be redundant with the very next step in the funnel — the actual checkout page, which independently and correctly re-fetches the service and determines/enforces prepayment (confirmed in the `book_nearest_slot` item directly below, which is the natural next step after this one). Not treated as a bug: the intent's job (who + when) and the checkout step's job (does this require payment, and how much) are cleanly separated, with no risk of the two disagreeing since checkout never trusts anything this intent returned about pricing — because it returns nothing about pricing at all.
- [x] **`book_nearest_slot`** — "book me the soonest opening" — confirm the resulting booking correctly carries prepayment requirements into the subsequent checkout step, for a `full`-prepayment service specifically (this is the ideal case to test with `pollin-clinic-3b7fb9d8`'s services, all `full`-mode). **Confirmed correct, live — carried through exactly as designed — but had to substitute a different full-prepayment service since `pollin-clinic-3b7fb9d8`'s own seed data turned out to be unusable for this specific test.** `pollin-clinic-3b7fb9d8`'s 3 active services (`Baby haircut`, `men's haircut`, `girl's haircut`) are indeed all `prepayment_mode: 'full'` as the checklist states, and `POST /public/pollin-clinic-3b7fb9d8/assistant` with `"book me the soonest opening for a men's haircut"` correctly classified to `book_nearest_slot` and correctly resolved the service (`serviceId` matched) — but returned `"No bookable slot for men's haircut on the requested day"`. Traced this to stale test data, not a bug: this business's only employee (Margarita Simonyan) has exactly 300 `scheduling_slots` rows, but every one of them falls in **2026-06-01 through 2026-06-05** — entirely in the past relative to "today" (2026-07-21/22 per this session's system clock). There is no code path bug here; there simply is no future availability to find for this specific business in the current seed snapshot.

  Rather than regenerate this business's entire schedule just to exercise a named test business that the checklist itself calls only "the ideal case" (not mandatory), substituted `gevgas-operations-7c299253`'s own `prepayment_mode: 'full'` service ("QA Concurrency Test", already used throughout this session, temporarily reactivated then reverted) — same prepayment mode, fresh/future slots. `POST /public/gevgas-operations-7c299253/assistant` with `"book me the soonest opening for QA Concurrency Test"` correctly classified to `book_nearest_slot`, resolved the nearest real slot (July 22 09:00 with Gevorg Gasparyan), and returned `success: true` with `navigate: { path: 'checkout', query: { serviceId, employeeId, startTime } }` — confirmed via source (`ai-payments.logic.ts:1226`) that this `navigate` payload never carries `price`/`prepaymentMode` fields at all; the checkout page is expected to independently resolve them by `serviceId`. Followed that exact navigate target live in the consumer-app (`consumer-assistant-navigate.util.ts`'s `checkout` branch resolves it to `/book/:serviceId?slot=...&date=...&employeeId=...`, the same `BookPage.tsx` route used everywhere else): the page correctly showed **Subtotal $40.00 / Due now $40.00** (full price, not partial/deposit) and the CTA read **"Pay & confirm booking"** — not a plain "Confirm booking" — confirming the full-prepayment requirement carried through end-to-end from `book_nearest_slot`'s resolved slot into the checkout step exactly as expected. No bug found. (Note, corroborating an existing finding elsewhere in this file: `book_nearest_slot` itself never creates a booking — its `success: true` means "found a slot and handed off to checkout," not "booked." The actual booking only gets created if the customer completes checkout — already flagged as a discrepancy worth knowing about in the `customer_clinic_compound` entry earlier in this document, where a compound orchestrator's "step succeeded" reporting didn't distinguish this from an actual persisted booking.)
- [x] **`get_booking_quote`** / **`get_package_quote`** / **`get_multi_service_quote`** — three parallel "how much would this cost" intents; confirm each returns the correct `amountDue` matching what the equivalent REST quote endpoint (already sweep-tested in API sweep M4/M5/M6) would return — this is a good spot to catch a conversational-layer amount-calculation drift from the REST layer. **Structurally impossible for these to drift — confirmed via source and empirically, live, for all 3.** All three logic handlers (`ai-payments.logic.ts:1592/1638/1720`) call the exact same `publicBookingService.quoteCheckout`/`quotePackageCheckout`/`quoteMultiServiceCheckout` methods the REST controller itself calls (confirmed via grep — identical method names, same service instance) — there is no separate conversational-layer calculation anywhere to drift. Verified with 3 live side-by-side comparisons anyway, since "architecturally guaranteed" and "empirically confirmed" aren't the same thing: `get_booking_quote` for "QA Concurrency Test" → AI: `"40 USD due now."`, REST `bookings/quote` → `amountDue: 40, currency: "USD"` — match. `get_package_quote` for "Massage Package" (all 5 lines `prepaymentMode: 'none'`) → AI: `"0 USD due now."`, REST `packages/quote` → `amountDue: 0` — match (also corroborates this session's earlier finding that this exact package correctly shows $0 due now in the real checkout UI). `get_multi_service_quote` for "Neck Massage" ($40, none) + "QA Concurrency Test" ($40, full) → AI: `"40 USD due now."`, REST `multi-service/quote` → `amountDue: 40` — match (only the full-prepayment line's amount, per the already-documented per-line-capped-sum rule). No drift found in any of the three. One unrelated, minor observation while testing: `get_booking_quote`'s and `get_multi_service_quote`'s service-name-to-serviceId resolution is phrasing-sensitive — "how much would QA Concurrency Test cost" failed to resolve the service at all (`"Which service would you like a quote for?"`) while "Give me a quote for QA Concurrency Test" worked correctly with the identical service name; not investigated further since it's a param-extraction/classifier-enrichment concern, not an amount-calculation one, and out of scope for this specific checklist item.
- [x] **`choose_payment_method`** — "what payment options do I have" / "can I pay online with card" / "do you accept cash" (real example prompts from `CASH_PAYMENT_CHECKOUT_PROMPTS`) — confirm it correctly reflects THIS business's actual `acceptCashPayments` + per-service `prepaymentMode`, not a generic answer; test once against a `full`-mode service (should say online-only) and once against a `none`-mode service with cash enabled (should offer both). **Confirmed correct on every axis tested, live.** Business-level toggle: called the exact fixture prompts ("What payment options do I have?", "Do you accept cash payments?") with `acceptCashPayments: true` → `"Payment options: Pay online (card), Pay cash at visit."`; flipped the business setting to `false` and re-ran the identical prompt → correctly changed to `"Online card payment only — cash at venue is not enabled. Options: Pay online (card)."` — a real, live-verified flip, not just a code read. Per-service `full`-mode (with cash re-enabled at the business level, to isolate the service-level gate specifically): `"What payment options do I have for QA Concurrency Test?"` → `"Pay online (card). QA Concurrency Test requires full payment online — cash at venue is not available for checkout."` — correctly online-only despite the business otherwise allowing cash, exactly as the checklist predicted. Per-service `none`-mode with cash enabled: `"What payment options do I have for full body massage?"` → `"For full body massage: Pay online (card) or Pay cash at visit."` — correctly offers both. All 4 live checks passed.

  **Found one real, reproducible classifier miss along the way (not part of the checklist's own ask, but hit while probing phrasing variants).** `"can I pay online with card for QA Concurrency Test"` — a natural paraphrase of one of the fixture prompts, just with a service name appended — does **not** classify to `choose_payment_method` (expected, since the classifier's own documented rule explicitly carves out named-service prompts to a different intent, `explain_payment_options_for_service`) but also doesn't land on that expected alternative either: it classifies to **`explain_stripe_checkout_currency`**, an intent about which currency Stripe charges in, with a response that doesn't actually answer whether the customer can pay online for that service. Reproduced twice, same result both times — a stable miss, not a one-off nondeterministic fluke. Not fixed (classifier-accuracy tuning is a large, separate surface already tracked extensively elsewhere in this document, e.g. the "5 unrelated provider-related prompts... collapse to the same wrong destination" entry) — flagged here as a concrete repro case for that broader, already-known category of issue.
- [x] **`pay_online`** — explicit card-payment selection mid-conversation. **Confirmed correct once given resolved slot context, live.** A single bare "pay online" prompt (no prior structured context) correctly fails clean — `"Pick a time slot first, then say pay online to open secure Stripe checkout."` — rather than guessing or erroring; plain conversational `history` text alone (a prior user/assistant text exchange establishing a slot) did **not** carry `serviceId`/`startTime`/`employeeId` forward into this turn's params either, confirming that slot context must arrive as structured data, not be re-inferred from chat transcript text on every turn. Supplied `serviceId`/`startTime`/`employeeId` directly via the request's `context` object instead (bypassing my own uncertainty about exactly how the real consumer-app widget threads state across turns) and got a fully correct result: `"Pay online with card for QA Concurrency Test Opening secure Stripe checkout for your selected time. Full prepayment is due now via Stripe."` — service correctly resolved, prepayment-mode-specific note correctly attached (this is `QA Concurrency Test`, a `full`-mode service), `sessionContext: { paymentMethod: 'online' }` correctly set for the client to remember, and a `navigate: { path: 'checkout', query: { serviceId, payment: 'online' } }` returned. **One minor observation, not investigated further**: the returned `navigate.query` only carried `serviceId`+`payment`, dropping the `startTime`/`employeeId` I'd supplied via `context` — per `buildPayOnlineCheckoutNavigate`'s source, those two fields are required together to include them in the navigate query, so either they didn't make it from `context` into the handler's `params` the way I passed them (a test-harness/plumbing question, since I'm not the real client and don't know the exact expected shape), or genuinely only `serviceId` survives cross-turn today. Not chased further since the core mechanism (resolve service, correctly gate on prepayment, hand off to checkout) is confirmed working.

  **Case (a) — found broken, now fixed (e2e-bug.188).** Live, before the fix: sent `"Confirm my payment"` with `context: { pendingCheckoutSessionId: "cs_test_..." }` set exactly as `ConsumerBookingAssistant.tsx`'s real `assistantContext` would — got `"Missing the Stripe checkout session to confirm."` anyway. Traced why: `handleConfirmStripePaymentLogic` only ever read `params.sessionId`; nothing anywhere in the codebase maps `pendingCheckoutSessionId` → `sessionId` for this intent (confirmed via grep — that field is only ever consumed by the *different*, non-mutating `resume_pending_payment` intent researched earlier this session). So the single most realistic real-world usage of this intent — a customer returning from Stripe and asking the assistant "did my payment go through?" while the app's own state already has the session tracked — **always failed**, regardless of whether the payment actually succeeded. Fixed with a one-line fallback: `params.sessionId ?? params.pendingCheckoutSessionId`. Re-tested live with the identical request: now correctly returns `"Payment confirmed — your booking is set."` with `sessionContext: { paymentMethod: 'online' }`. Added a regression test (`ai-payments.logic.spec.ts`) covering the missing-sessionId clarify path, the explicit-`sessionId` success path, the new `pendingCheckoutSessionId` fallback path, and the confirm-failure path; all pass. `tsc --noEmit` clean on the touched files; the broader jest run shows only 3 pre-existing, unrelated failures (confirmed via `git stash` — identical before and after this fix).

  **Case (b) confirmed correct, live** (after finding the right phrasing — my own paraphrases kept landing on wrong intents, see below): the exact fixture prompt `"Confirm my payment"` with zero context correctly returns `{success: false, summary: "Missing the Stripe checkout session to confirm."}` — a clean clarify, never a crash or a guessed session.

  **Case (c) confirmed correct, live, incidentally** — re-confirming an already-completed real session (`cs_test_a1RJz...`, fully paid and confirmed earlier this session) via the assistant returned `success: true` again cleanly, and the DB shows exactly one booking row tied to that session both before and after — no duplicate created by the repeat confirm.

  **Case (d) — deliberately not customer-scoped, and this is consistent with the REST layer, not a new gap.** Read `confirmCheckoutSession` (`booking-payment.service.ts:1094`): its signature is `(slug, sessionId)` — there is no customerId parameter anywhere for it to check, and this is the exact same method the ordinary checkout-return flow calls for every one of this session's real Stripe payments. The security model here is "possession of the high-entropy Stripe session ID is the credential" (matching the return URL's own `session_id` query param — never displayed to any other customer, no more guessable than the token). So unlike `receipt_status`'s bookingId (a comparatively low-entropy, more incidentally-exposed DB UUID with no established bearer-token model anywhere else in the app), `confirm_stripe_payment` not checking customer identity is architecturally consistent with how the whole checkout-confirmation system already works, not a gap introduced by the AI layer. No fix needed.

Combined with the `explain_stripe_checkout_currency` misclassifications already flagged twice in earlier entries in this section, that's now 6 distinct reproducible misclassifications in this one payments-classifier neighborhood across this testing pass alone — a strong, repeated pattern, not isolated noise. Not fixed here (same broader, already-tracked classifier-accuracy category), but the volume specifically concentrated around payment-confirmation phrasing is worth flagging as a priority within that category, given how much real-world reliability rides on exactly this intent.

#### Compound / multi-step payment prompts

- [x] `isPaymentsCompoundPrompt` — a single prompt combining multiple payment actions (e.g., "book the 2pm slot and pay online") — confirm the compound splitter correctly segments this into sequential actions rather than misclassifying as one. **Found a real, deterministic bug: cross-domain payments compounds silently drop the non-payments half instead of segmenting it.** Live-tested the checklist's own example, `"book the 2pm slot and pay online"` → classified as a single, non-compound `pay_online` action: `"Pick a time slot first, then say pay online to open secure Stripe checkout."` — the booking half is silently discarded, not even acknowledged. Reproduced identically with the segments reversed (`"pay online and book the 2pm slot"`) — same result. Traced the root cause in `decomposePaymentsCompoundPrompt` (`ai-payments.util.ts:1167`): `COMPOUND_SPLIT`'s regex *does* correctly split the raw string into 2 segments (`"book the 2pm slot"`, `"pay online"`) since `and\s+(?=...)` matches before "pay" (a boundary word). But each segment is then run through `classifyPaymentsSegment` (`ai-payments.util.ts:1011`), which only recognizes payments-domain sub-intents plus one narrow booking special case, `isBookNearestSlotPrompt` — and "book the **2pm** slot" fails that check (confirmed via code read, `ai-payments.util.ts:361`: `isBookNearestSlotPrompt` requires a *flexible*-slot cue like nearest/soonest/next/earliest/asap; a literal clock time like "2pm" is a different, non-payments booking action it has no knowledge of). The unclassifiable segment returns `null` and is silently filtered out (`if (step) steps.push(step)`), so only 1 step survives — which means `isPaymentsCompoundPrompt` (gated on `decomposePaymentsCompoundPrompt(...).length > 1`) reports "not compound" even though the raw split found 2 segments, so the whole pipeline falls back to classifying the *entire original string* as one segment, which greedily matches "pay online" anywhere in the text. **Contrast — same-domain payments compounds work correctly**: re-tested with two payments-only actions in one prompt (`"check my gift card balance for code GCM-1234 and apply the gift card code at checkout"` → correctly split into `compound_intent`, stopped at step 1 on a legitimate "gift card not found" business-logic failure, not a classification failure; `"explain the checkout total and then pay online"` → same, correctly split into 2 steps). So the splitter itself is fine — the gap is specifically that `classifyPaymentsSegment` has no fallback path for booking-domain segments (specific-time bookings, named-slot bookings, etc.) that legitimately co-occur with a payment action in one sentence. This is a deterministic code-logic bug (not LLM temperature noise) — reproduced identically across repeat/reordered calls. **Not fixed here**: a proper fix requires either teaching `classifyPaymentsSegment` to recognize (or pass through) non-payments booking segments, or restructuring the higher-level orchestration (`intent-decomposition.util.ts`, which already juggles ~20 domain-specific compound decomposers) to try multiple domains' segment classifiers per-segment and merge results, rather than delegating whole-prompt decomposition to a single domain's decomposer — both are meaningfully larger, cross-cutting changes than this pass's other fixes, so flagged with full root cause rather than patched in place. **Real-world impact**: any customer combining a specific-time booking request with a payment instruction in one sentence ("book the 2pm slot and pay online", a completely natural thing to say) silently loses the booking half and gets a confusing "pick a time slot first" message despite having just specified one.

**Second, independently-discovered live instance of the same bug class (user-reported, not from the checklist)**: `"How much is a hairstyle and who is available at 2pm"` → classified as a single `check_providers_for_service` action, completely dropping the price question — no mention of cost anywhere in the response, only the availability list. Confirmed `explain_service_price` alone works correctly (`"How much is a hairstyle"` → `"hairstyle — 60 min · 15 USD..."`), so this is the same silent-drop mechanism, not a broken price handler. Root cause identical in shape: `COMPOUND_SPLIT`'s regex correctly splits on `"and who"` (`"who"` is a boundary word), giving 2 segments (`"How much is a hairstyle"`, `"who is available at 2pm"`), but `classifyPaymentsSegment` has no case for `explain_service_price` at all — it's only ever referenced in this file's single-action *rescue* path (`ai-payments.util.ts:854`), never in the segment classifier — so segment 1 returns `null` and is filtered out, only 1 step survives, `isPaymentsCompoundPrompt` reports "not compound", and the fallback single-segment classification of the full raw string matches `check_providers_for_service` (since "who is available" is still present in the full text), discarding the price question entirely. (params.serviceName ? undefined : session.serviceId)`). This means a customer who already picked a `full`-mode service earlier in the conversation, then later says something like "actually, skip online payment for the girls haircut" (a totally natural, slightly-imprecise restatement — no apostrophe, wrong case, etc.), gets the reliable `session.serviceId` silently *suppressed* in favor of re-resolving by the malformed name — which then fails to match, `resolveService` returns nothing, the full-mode gate never fires, and the cash-skip is wrongly allowed for a service that legally requires full online payment. Flagging with root cause and a suggested narrower fix direction: have `resolveService` fall back to `params.serviceId`/session context specifically when the name-based lookup comes back empty, rather than changing the shared merge helper's behavior for all intents. #### Structural note: native-only features are un-testable via the browser tool used for every prior test pass this session

`use-deep-link-router.ts` opens with `if (!Capacitor.isNativePlatform()) return;` — the entire deep-link router (6 distinct URL patterns), native push, and the home-screen-widget sync below are **gated off entirely in a browser**, meaning nothing tested so far via `mcp__Claude_Browser__*` could have exercised any of them, regardless of how thoroughly the rest of the app was clicked through. This whole category needs an actual iOS/Android device or simulator with a real Capacitor native build, not just the web dev server — worth flagging as a hard methodology limit, not a "case to add," before listing the cases themselves.

That downstream logic is what I could — and did — test live: called `parseCheckoutReturnRoute` + `resolveCheckoutReturnNavigationPath` directly against the real running module (`javascript_tool` → `import('/src/lib/consumer-checkout-return.util.ts')`, not a reimplementation) with realistic `optischedule://book/{slug}/...` URLs for all 4 native-scheme kinds that actually exist in source today (package/multi/gift_card, plus a 4th, `single`, added by the already-fixed e2e-bug.18) — every one parsed and resolved to the correct in-app path: package → `/s/{slug}/book/packages/pkg-123/checkout?session_id=...`; multi → `/s/{slug}/book/multi/checkout?session_id=...`; gift_card → `/s/{slug}/gift-cards/checkout?session_id=...`; single → `/s/{slug}/book/svc-abc-123?session_id=...`. Also live-navigated the browser to one of these resolved paths directly to confirm the destination page itself renders correctly end-to-end (not just that the string looks right) — covered under the manage-booking item below, same verification method. **What this does NOT prove, and cannot prove via this session's browser-only tooling**: whether `Capacitor.isNativePlatform()` correctly gates true in a real native build, whether `getLaunchUrl()` actually returns the launching URL on a genuine cold start vs. `appUrlOpen` firing on warm-resume, or whether the OS/App-Store actually associates the `optischedule://` scheme with this app at all — those require an actual iOS/Android device or simulator with a real Capacitor native build, exactly as this section's own methodology note says. Live-navigated the browser to that resolved path against the clinic-vertical business used for the item above and confirmed a real, correctly-rendered home page ("QA Test Clinic", with "Book an appointment" / "Lab collection to book" / "Salon profile" / "My account" — the clinic-specific "Lab collection to book" entry confirming this business's vertical-specific features are genuinely wired, not just a generic template). Same native-only caveat applies to the actual OS-level share-link tap itself.
- [x] **Deferred-slug-after-install flow** (`stashSlugForInstall`/`consumeDeferredSlug`) — this is the actual mechanism behind `frontend`'s `/get-app/[slug]` handoff page found earlier: a customer without the app taps a web link, gets redirected to the app store, installs, and on first native launch (no launch URL from the OS) the app should still resolve the originally-intended salon from storage. This is a multi-step, cross-app-boundary flow that's easy to get wrong and hasn't been tested even conceptually until now. **Found and confirmed a severe, root-caused bug: this flow cannot work at all, on any real device, as currently implemented — it's not an edge case, it's architecturally broken.** Traced the full chain: `frontend`'s `GetAppClient` (`app/get-app/[slug]/get-app-client.tsx:25`) calls `saveDeferredInstallLink(...)`, which (`deferred-install-link.util.ts:140`) writes to plain browser `localStorage` on whatever origin `frontend` is served from (the phone's system Safari/Chrome, since this page runs *before* the app exists). The native consumer-app's `consumeDeferredSlug()` (`deep-link.ts:82`, called from `use-deep-link-router.ts:95` when `getLaunchUrl()` returns nothing) reads from `localStorage` too — but `consumer-app`'s `capacitor.config.ts` (`webDir: 'dist'`) confirms it's a fully bundled, locally-loaded native app (Capacitor's own local scheme — `capacitor://localhost` on iOS, `https://localhost` on Android), which is a **completely separate storage sandbox** from the system browser where the pre-install page ran. `localStorage` never crosses that boundary on a real device — this is standard, unavoidable mobile-platform behavior, not a config bug that can be tuned away. **Demonstrated this empirically, not just by architecture reasoning**: started the actual `frontend` dev server, navigated to `/get-app/gevgas-operations-7c299253?serviceId=...&src=qr`, and confirmed via `localStorage.getItem(...)` that `saveDeferredInstallLink` correctly wrote the expected payload on `frontend`'s origin (`http://localhost:3000`) — the write side works exactly as designed. Then checked `consumer-app`'s origin (`http://localhost:5174`) and confirmed the same keys (`consumer_deferred_install`, `consumer_deferred_slug`) are `null` there — completely invisible, as same-origin-policy guarantees. This dev-server port difference is actually an *easier* boundary to cross than the real one (a genuine native app-install has zero shared storage with the system browser under any circumstance, whereas two localhost ports could theoretically be worked around with clever tooling) — so if it fails here, it fails even harder on a real device. **Net effect in production**: the exact scenario this checklist item describes — customer taps a web link, has no app, gets sent to the store, installs, opens the app for the first time with no OS-delivered launch URL — will **always** land on the generic app-open experience with zero salon context, silently dropping the entire attribution/deep-link intent (slug, serviceId, referralCode, date/slot/employeeId, install-source campaign data) that `frontend` worked to capture. This isn't a "needs a real device to find out" gap — it's confirmable and confirmed to be broken by the storage mechanism alone, no device required. **Fix direction**: real deferred-deep-linking requires either a server-side matching service (Firebase Dynamic Links / App Links with fingerprint matching, or a paid service like Branch/AppsFlyer), or platform-native workarounds — iOS's `UIPasteboard` (write the slug to the system clipboard before redirecting to the App Store; the freshly-launched app reads the clipboard once on first open) or Android's **Play Install Referrer API** (the Play Store natively passes referrer data through to the installed app, no clipboard hack needed). None of these are present anywhere in the codebase today (confirmed via grep — no clipboard, no Install Referrer, no Firebase Dynamic Links integration). Not fixed here — this is a meaningfully large feature build, not a patch.
- [x] **Home-screen widget sync** (`useHomeScreenWidgetSync`, tagged `adopt-4.7`) — iOS WidgetKit / Android App Widget showing a booking snapshot; needs a real device home screen to verify at all, and specifically needs verifying the widget updates when a booking is cancelled/rescheduled/completed, not just on creation. **The data-computation logic is confirmed correct for all 3 named transitions; found one real, confirmed architectural gap in how/when it actually refreshes.** Same testing pattern as the earlier native-only items: the actual native write (`syncHomeScreenWidgetSnapshot`, `home-screen-widget-native.ts`) is gated behind `Capacitor.isNativePlatform()` and calls into genuine, fully-built native code (`HomeScreenWidgetPlugin.swift`/`.java`, `OptiScheduleWidget.swift`, `ConsumerHomeWidgetProvider.java` — a real implementation, not a stub), but the upstream snapshot-building logic (`buildHomeScreenWidgetSnapshot`, `pickNextUpcomingBooking`, `pickLastCompletedBooking`, all in `home-screen-widget.util.ts`) is pure and testable. Called it live against the running module for all 3 named transitions: a `confirmed` future booking → correctly shown as `nextAppointment`; the same booking marked `cancelled` → `nextAppointment: null` (correctly excluded — `pickNextUpcomingBooking` filters to `{confirmed, pending}` only); the same booking with an updated `startTime` (reschedule) → still correctly shown as `nextAppointment`, now keyed off the new time; the same booking with `status: 'completed'` and a past `startTime` → correctly moved out of `nextAppointment` and into `quickRebook` instead, with a correctly-built rebook deep link (`optischedule://book/{slug}/book/{serviceId}?date=...&slot=...&rebook=1&rebookBookingId=...&rebookSource=widget`) once a `serviceId` was included in the test fixture (an initial run without one produced a `book/undefined` URL — traced to my own incomplete test data, not a code bug, and confirmed clean on retry with `serviceId` set). **The real, confirmed gap — direct answer to the checklist's "not just on creation" concern**: traced how the resync is actually triggered and found it's entirely app-lifecycle-driven, with no independent channel. `useHomeScreenWidgetSync` is mounted broadly (`SalonTabChrome.tsx`, the shared tab-bar shell, plus `AccountPage.tsx` directly) so it re-syncs the widget whenever the `bookings` prop changes *while the app's JS is alive* — on mount, on any prop change, and via an `appStateChange` listener that invalidates the bookings query when the app is foregrounded. Grepped for any silent-push, background-fetch, or `BGTaskScheduler`/`WorkManager`-style mechanism tied to widget refresh — found none. **Consequence**: if the *customer* cancels/reschedules from within the app, the widget correctly updates on the next foreground/background cycle (or immediately, if the mutation's own query invalidation fires while still in the foreground). But if the *provider* cancels, reschedules, or marks the visit complete from their own dashboard while the customer's app is fully closed, the customer's home-screen widget will show stale information until they next open the consumer app themselves — there's no push-driven background refresh to catch third-party-initiated changes. This may be an acceptable, common trade-off for a simple widget (many apps' widgets only refresh on next open), but it's a real, confirmed limitation worth being explicit about rather than assuming the widget is always live. Same hard native-device-required caveat as prior items applies to the actual on-screen widget rendering/refresh-cadence itself.

#### Third sign-in method never tested: phone/SMS OTP (only Google was planned before)

`ConsumerSignInProvider = 'google' | 'apple' | 'phone'` (`use-consumer-one-tap-sign-in.ts`) — this session's plans only ever mention Google. Apple and phone are equally real, distinct paths.

- [ ] Phone sign-in happy path — enter phone, receive SMS OTP, enter code, sign in
- [ ] `isValidConsumerPhone`/`normalizeConsumerPhone` — international phone number formats, with/without country code, with formatting characters (spaces, dashes, parens) — confirm normalization is consistent with what the backend expects (cross-check against **api-bug.1**'s area of the codebase generally being fragile around string formats)
- [x] `sanitizeSmsOtpCode` — OTP entry with extra whitespace/non-digit characters pasted in (common when copy-pasting from an SMS app). **The sanitize function itself is correct — but this, and the two items below, all trace back to one root finding: phone/OTP sign-in is entirely disabled and stubbed in this build, not merely hard to test.** Live-tested `sanitizeSmsOtpCode` directly against the running module with realistic garbage inputs: `"  1 2 3   4 5 6  "` (pasted with spaces) → `"123456"`; `"123-456"` → `"123456"`; `"OTP: 123456!"` → `"123456"`; a 14-digit over-length paste → correctly truncated to 6; and the single most realistic real-world case — long-pressing to copy an *entire* SMS message body, `"Your OptiSchedule code is: 482913. Do not share it."` — correctly extracted just `"482913"`. The sanitizer itself has no bug.
- [x] Wrong OTP code — error messaging (candidate for yet another e2e-bug.3 instance). **Not applicable — there is no real OTP verification to produce a wrong-code error at all.** Read `useConsumerOneTapSignIn`'s `verifyPhoneCode` (`use-consumer-one-tap-sign-in.ts:91`): if the sanitized OTP is non-empty, it unconditionally calls `setMessage('Phone sign-in is not configured in this build.')` — a static stub string, not a real backend verification call, with no distinction whatsoever between a right code, a wrong code, or a malformed one. `sendPhoneCode` (line 82) is the same shape: validates the phone format locally, then always shows the same "not configured" stub regardless of input. Neither function ever calls a Stripe/Firebase/backend endpoint, so there's no server error to leak in the first place — this specific e2e-bug.3 candidacy doesn't apply because nothing real is happening yet to go wrong.
- [x] OTP expiry / resend flow — never located a resend mechanism; needs its own discovery pass. **Confirmed: there is no resend mechanism, and there never could be one yet — the entire phone-sign-in UI is unreachable in the live app today.** Traced the root cause: `LoginPage.tsx` gates its whole phone-auth block behind `{isPhoneSignInAvailable() ? (...) : null}`, and `services/phone-auth.ts` hardcodes `isPhoneSignInAvailable()` to return `false` unconditionally — a 3-line stub file, not a real feature-flag or config check. Confirmed live: cleared local storage to force a genuinely signed-out state and loaded the real `/login` page — the rendered page shows only `"Continue with Google"`; no phone number field, no "Send code" button, no OTP step, nothing. Read the full phone-step JSX anyway (`LoginPage.tsx:148-181`) for when/if this ever gets enabled: it has a "Send code" step, an OTP-entry step with "Verify" and "Use a different number" (which resets back to the phone step — not a resend), and genuinely **no "Resend code" button or expiry countdown anywhere in the markup**. So this finding holds either way: today, the whole feature is invisible to real users (not just hard to test — actually shipped disabled); and even if/when `isPhoneSignInAvailable()` is flipped on, the currently-written UI still has no resend affordance and the hook layer has no real send/verify/expiry logic behind it at all (see the two items above) — this would need real implementation work (an actual SMS-OTP provider integration, a resend cooldown, a real verify-code backend call), not just a flag flip.
- [x] Apple Sign-In happy path and failure/cancellation handling — entirely unplanned until now, same treatment as Google needs. **Same shape as phone sign-in above — Apple Sign-In is also hardcoded off, not implemented.** `services/apple-auth.ts` hardcodes `isAppleSignInAvailable()` to `false` (a 3-line stub, identical pattern to phone), so `LoginPage.tsx`'s `{isAppleSignInAvailable() ? (...) : null}` never renders the Apple button in the real app (confirmed live in the same signed-out `/login` page check done for phone auth — only "Continue with Google" shows). Underneath, `signInWithApple()` (`use-consumer-one-tap-sign-in.ts:78`) just sets a static `"Apple sign-in is not configured in this build."` message, and the service's own `getAppleIdToken()` throws immediately if ever called (`"Apple sign-in is not configured in this build"`). So there's no happy path, no failure path, and no cancellation path to test — none of them are wired to anything real yet. One reassuring thing found while tracing this: the **backend** already has real, shared, provider-agnostic logic ready for whenever this gets implemented — `PublicCustomerAuthService.loginWithOAuthIdToken(slug, idToken, provider: 'google' | 'apple', ...)` (`public-customer-auth.service.ts:225`) already handles both `'google'` and `'apple'` as first-class provider values, correctly matches/creates the customer record by lowercased email within the business scope (`LOWER(customer.email) = :email`), and stores `metadata.authProvider`/`{provider}Sub` per-provider — so the backend identity model is already sound for this; it's purely the frontend (`getAppleIdToken()`, `isAppleSignInAvailable()`) that's stubbed.
- [x] `claimPendingReferralAfterSignIn` — confirms a referral code entered PRE-signin (as a guest) correctly attaches once the customer actually signs in — a timing-dependent case that's easy to silently break. **The core happy path works correctly; found a real, confirmed bug in the cleanup/retry semantics that lets an already-claimed code resurface.** Live-tested the full orchestration directly against the running module (`claimPendingReferralAfterSignIn` takes its `claim` callback as a parameter, so this is genuinely testable without a real backend call): captured a referral code as a guest via `captureReferralFromSearch('?ref=abcd1234', slug)`, confirmed it persists (`readPendingReferralCode` → `"ABCD1234"`), then simulated the post-signin claim — attach succeeded, pending code correctly cleared afterward. Also tested a network-error path (`claim` throws) → pending code correctly **preserved** (so a failed claim attempt can retry on a later sign-in) — good, resilient design. **The confirmed bug**: `savePendingReferralCode` (`consumer-referral.util.ts:24`) writes the referral code to **two** places — the dedicated `consumer_pending_referral:{slug}` key, *and* as a side effect into the shared deferred-install-link payload (`consumer_deferred_install`, via `saveDeferredInstallLink`). But `clearPendingReferralCode` (called after every claim attempt, success or `attached:false`) only clears the **first** location — it never touches the deferred-install-link's `referralCode` field, which has no TTL check anywhere in `deferred-install-link.util.ts` (confirmed via grep) and persists indefinitely. Since `resolvePendingReferralForClaim` (the function `claimPendingReferralAfterSignIn` actually calls) reads `readPendingReferralCode(slug) ?? peekDeferredInstallLink()?.referralCode`, the already-claimed code becomes the *fallback* value forever. Reproduced directly: after a successful attach+clear, `resolvePendingReferralForClaim(slug)` still returned the same code that was just claimed. **Real-world impact**: if `claimPendingReferralAfterSignIn` is ever invoked again for the same slug/browser (e.g., customer signs out and back in, or any other flow that calls this same completion path) after a successful claim, it will silently re-submit the exact same already-consumed referral code to the backend's claim API — at best a harmless no-op if the backend is idempotent about already-attached codes, at worst a confusing repeated-claim error the customer never asked for and can't clear themselves (there's no UI to inspect/clear this state). Not fixed here — the fix is straightforward (have `clearPendingReferralCode` also clear/null out the deferred-install-link's `referralCode` field, or have `claimPendingReferralAfterSignIn` call `consumeDeferredInstallLink()` instead of the narrower `clearPendingReferralCode()`), but flagging rather than patching given the shared deferred-install-link state is touched by several other flows (install attribution, service/date/slot resume) that would need re-checking for regressions.
- [x] All three sign-in methods' interaction with `recordActiveTenant`/`setCustomerSession` — confirm signing in via one method, then later via a different method with the same underlying identity (e.g., same email via Google then Apple), doesn't create two separate customer records or cause a conflict. **Currently untestable in practice, for a good reason: only one of the three methods actually exists today.** Given both Apple and phone sign-in are confirmed non-functional stubs (see the two items above), there is no second *real* provider to sign in with and trigger a same-identity conflict — Google is the only method that ever calls a real backend endpoint right now, so "sign in via one method, then a different method, same identity" cannot occur in this build regardless of how it's tested. `recordActiveTenant`/`setCustomerSession` (`customer-auth.ts:41,76`) themselves are simple, correct, per-slug localStorage writers with no cross-provider logic of their own — the real identity-matching happens server-side. Checked that server-side logic anyway, since it's what would matter the moment Apple sign-in ships: `loginWithOAuthIdToken` (referenced in the Apple item above) is already provider-agnostic and matches/creates customers by **email**, business-scoped — so a customer signing in via Google then later via Apple with the same email *would* correctly resolve to the same customer record once Apple sign-in is real, per this code path. This is a reassuring, forward-looking confirmation rather than a live test of the actual scenario — genuinely re-test this once Apple (or phone) sign-in is wired up for real, since today there is nothing to conflict with.

#### Session / token lifecycle (never explicitly planned)

- [x] JWT expiry mid-session — customer has the app open across the token's expiry boundary; does a subsequent action fail gracefully (re-prompt sign-in) or crash/hang? **No crash, no hang — but found a real, concrete bug: one section silently lies instead of degrading gracefully like its siblings.** Simulated expiry live by writing a garbage token (`localStorage.setItem('consumer_token_{slug}', 'expired.invalid.jwt.garbage')`) and loading the real Account page. Confirmed via network inspection that `/me/bookings` genuinely returns a clean `401 Unauthorized` (not a connection error — verified this distinction after an unrelated backend restart briefly muddied the first attempt with `ERR_CONNECTION_REFUSED`, then re-ran cleanly once the server was back). Result: the header still shows the cached name/email (from localStorage, never re-validated against the 401), **Notification preferences** and **Waitlist** sections both correctly show an honest degradation message (`"Could not load notification preferences."` / `"Could not load. Check your connection and try again."`) — good, no crash, no raw error, clear signal something's wrong. But **My appointments** shows `"No bookings yet."` — the *exact same empty state* a genuinely zero-booking customer would see, with zero indication the fetch actually failed with a 401. This is worse than a generic error: a customer whose token silently expired mid-session, who actually has real upcoming appointments, would see this and reasonably conclude their appointments vanished or were never booked, rather than realizing they just need to sign in again. Root cause not fully traced to a single line (would need to find wherever `useQuery(['bookings', slug])`'s error/empty-state branching lives and see why it doesn't distinguish "0 real results" from "fetch failed"), but the inconsistency with the two sibling sections on the same page — same root cause (401), different, correct handling — is a clear, reproducible signal something in this one section's error path needs the same "show an honest error" treatment its neighbors already have.
- [x] Silent token refresh, if one exists — needs a discovery pass on whether `customer-auth.ts` has any refresh mechanism at all, or whether expiry just forces a full re-login. **Confirmed: none exists.** Read the entire file (`customer-auth.ts`, 190 lines) — it's purely a thin localStorage wrapper (`getCustomerToken`/`setCustomerSession`/`clearCustomerSession`/tenant-tracking helpers); no refresh token concept, no expiry-checking, no token decoding anywhere. Also checked for a global HTTP-layer safety net: `services/public-api.ts`'s axios instance has no `interceptors` configured at all (grepped for the literal word — zero matches), and the app's single `QueryClient` (`main.tsx:28`) only sets `{ retry: 2, staleTime: 30_000 }` with no `onError`/auth-aware retry logic. The only 401-specific handling anywhere in the consumer-app is in `ManageBookingPage.tsx` — but that's for the unrelated guest manage-token flow, not the customer JWT. So today, expiry is handled entirely per-page (inconsistently, per the item above) rather than by any shared refresh or redirect-to-login mechanism — there is no silent refresh, and there's also no *forced* full re-login prompt either; the app just keeps running with a dead token until the customer notices something's off or manually signs out/in.
- [x] Signing out on one device/tab and the effect (if any) on a session open elsewhere. **Confirmed: no cross-tab sync exists — a stale signed-in tab stays signed-in until it independently re-reads storage (e.g. on navigation/reload).** Grepped the whole consumer-app for any `storage` event listener tied to auth (the standard mechanism for same-browser cross-tab awareness) — the only hit anywhere in the codebase is in `AccessibilityBootstrap.tsx`, unrelated to auth. `clearCustomerSession`/`setCustomerSession` are plain synchronous localStorage writes with no `BroadcastChannel`, no custom event dispatch, nothing that would notify a sibling tab. Practical effect: if a customer signs out in Tab A, a Tab B that's already open and rendered stays showing the signed-in UI with its already-fetched data until it happens to re-mount or re-read storage on its own (e.g., the customer navigates within Tab B, or reloads it) — there's no proactive "you've been signed out elsewhere" push. This is a common, often-acceptable trade-off for apps without a real-time session layer (rather than a severe bug), but is worth being explicit about since nothing today would stop Tab B from continuing to show/attempt actions against a session Tab A just tore down.
